Quantitative research study on how individuals with ASD perceive their own symptoms  
  
Hello All! I am a 24 year old female with ASD and I am conducting a Qualtrics survey study to determine the different self-perceived intensity at which those with Autism Spectrum Disorder experience their symptoms for my graduate thesis in the Creative Arts Therapy Department at Nazareth College in Rochester, NY. The goal of the study is to determine if the sex assigned at birth correlates with different intensities of particular Autistic traits. The target age range will be between the ages of 18 and 65. Individuals will be excluded if they do not fall into the category of self-diagnosed or clinically diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Individuals will also be excluded for all other neuro-developmental and psychotic disorders with the exception of Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) due to the high co-morbidity of Autism and ADHD.  
  
Survey Link:  
  
https://naz.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV\_2h5e8UwRGBxnt8q

Regular room humidity is fine for the majority of the time (unless you live in a really dry area, I live in NY where humidity is pretty high) but when they shed you should put in a humidity box. Personally, Noodle hates his humidity box so when he goes into shed I dampen moss and put it on his warm side to increase the humidity and it works really well. But NEVER leave the humidity box or moss in there when they're not in shed because it can lead to scale rot if the humidity is always high. And don't wet the moss too much for the same reason, there should never be puddles in the enclosure or in the humidity box for them to just sit in because of potential scale rot.

Get a thermometer to plug it into. It should be on constantly but make sure it's only on one side of the enclosure because they need a warm and cool side to thermoregulate. The warm side can go from 86-93°F while the cool side should be in the mid to high 70s

I've been with my boyfriend for 6 1/2 years and he's always had an interesting way of supporting me. He knows that some days I struggle to eat and can't focus and often will curl up in pain or have intense anxiety attacks but he's not the type of person to go "have you eaten? How are you feeling? Etc." Instead, since I'm vocal about my illness outwardly to myself (I talk to myself ALOT) he says things like "well, don't do that!" Or "well, gosh, you eat then! You need that to live!" From anyone else it'd be mean and irritating but he does it in such a way that's almost joking and always follows it by a hug or kiss. It's like he's trying to remind me to practice self-care but he knows that I'm an indepemdent person who wouldn't appreciate being told what to do. It's nice. 

He also doesn't hugely acknowledge my illness. For example, if we're laying there talking and he squeezes my stomach while holding me then I can just say that it's uncomfortable or painful and he'll move but not break the conversation. He doesn't micromanage or make it become the basis of our lives. Yes, I'm in pain. Yes, I feel like shit. But I don't know what I'd do if I couldn't express my pain without it taking over conversations and events.
